subject: 🤑 Banker payday!
body_text:
96 
Plus: And now the hard part | Friday, November 20, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
 Presented By Capital One 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Nov 20, 2026
 
 
 🥳 Friday! It'll be hard to top yesterday's insane hype over the most anticipated debut of the year. But Grand Theft Auto VI seems to have been worth the 13-year wait. Oh, and there was that big AI IPO too. More on that below from both of us.

 One thing is clear: Anthropic's IPO yesterday didn't magically turn around investor jitters on AI. (The S&P ended down 2%.)

 Futures are pointing to another weak open today, led by, you guessed it, Big Tech, after Korean markets took another tumble overnight. Oh, and ANT itself is down by more than 7% in premarket trading. "Simple choice really, get busy living or get busy dying." In 1,075 words, a 4-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: Banks feast on ANT offering
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios The Anthropic IPO brought in a tidy payday for Wall Street, with investment bankers raking in $550 million in underwriting fees.

 Why it matters: The enormous windfall comes as Wall Street wraps up a year that already has bankers anticipating hefty bonuses.

 Behind the scenes: The first day of an IPO is a Super Bowl-level marketing event for a new company and its bankers, heavily engineered to generate hype and drive interest.

 When you hear that an IPO was "oversubscribed" — meaning demand exceeded the supply of shares as was the case with Anthropic — that just means the bankers did their job. "The whole point of having an underwriter is to have an oversubscribed deal," says Paul Kedrosky, a venture capitalist and long-time tech investor. Anthropic delivered on the hype for day one. The stock opened at $111.50 — a 34% lift from its $83 offering price — before closing at $97.17.

 The company closed at a market cap of about $1.25 trillion, a big number but not enough to vault it into the top 10 most valuable public firms. The big picture: There was hope that a big pop (an Anthropop, mayhaps) would lift the AI trade. It did not.

 The tech-heavy Nasdaq finished the day down 2.25% and is -9.6% for the past 30 days. Follow the money: Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs were the lead bankers on the IPO — and will take home roughly 41% of the $550 million in fees, per the WSJ . The other 20 banks on the deal share the rest.

 Anthropic, like SpaceX, negotiated low underwriting fees — less than a 1% commission on the total offering — far below typical commissions for big IPOs. But since the deal was so big, the payday was still a whopper. Flashback: When Visa went public in 2008, it paid $550.2 million in underwriting fees, about a 2.8% commission, per its SEC filing .

 Zoom in: There was likely more on the table for the bankers, who get to decide which investors receive those scarce in-demand $83 shares, says University of Florida finance professor Jay Ritter, who studies IPOs. 

 Valuable IPO allocations can help banks attract trading business. And typically, sales and trading commissions go up for the quarter when a deal gets done, Ritter says. Zoom out: The payoff is only one piece of what's been a big year for the banks, says Chris Connors, a managing director at compensation consulting firm Johnson Associates.

 Bonuses for the bankers who work on equity deals are projected to rise by as much as 30% this year, per the firm's numbers . Between the lines: Perhaps even more important than the cash the IPO generates is the marketing, says Connors. 

 Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs get to be the two lead underwriters on Anthropic and SpaceX — the "biggest IPOs of all time." The branding is as important as the revenue, he adds. What to watch: The story for public-market investors has yet to be written. Historically, IPO stocks haven't been great bets. 

 They've underperformed the broader market by an average of 20 percentage points in the three years after their first day of trading, per Ritter's research. The bottom line: One of Anthropic's stated goals is the long-term benefit of humanity, and the company also warns it could destroy humanity. The jury's still out on those. 

 Meantime, the bankers and company insiders can count their winnings.

 A $25M commitment to expand access to homeownership 
   
 
 
 
   
 
 Meet the 10 finalists for Capital One and the Capital One Foundation's $25M philanthropic initiative.


 The goal: Scale solutions that expand housing supply, lower the cost of building or buying and help more people prepare for homeownership.


 Learn more. 


 
   
   
 
2. Anthropic is public, but now comes the hard part
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios With its IPO done and dusted, Anthropic's shareholders will be watching its progress toward becoming a business that doesn't need constant capital infusions from investors and vendors. 

 Why it matters: Anthropic — along with OpenAI — is at the heart of the industry that's dominated the equity and debt markets for the last four years. 

 Much of the AI infrastructure boom is ultimately aimed at supplying compute power to these two companies. Yes, but : The bill for that data center investment will start to come due over the next few years.

 And Anthropic and OpenAI are going to have to pay for quite a bit of it. How it works: Anthropic has covered much of its computing costs thus far by selling parts of itself off to compute vendors like Amazon and Alphabet and by raising more cash from other investors.

 But eventually the company's core business will have to generate enough money to pay on its own. Case in point: Anthropic's filings say it is on the hook for roughly $900 billion in spending commitments — mostly for data centers and computing power — with about half of that due before the end of 2030. 

 After the IPO, Anthropic is expected to have over $200 billion in cash and short-term investments in the bank, which should buy it some time. But sales will have go a lot higher to just cover those costs, let alone deliver the profits Anthropic's new shareholders are hoping for. By the numbers: As the chart above shows, Anthropic posted a loss of roughly $23 billion on revenue of nearly $17 billion in the third quarter. 

 It's true that much of that loss stems from a non-cash accounting charge of almost $22 billion. But even the more favorable metric of operating income — which strips out the paper losses and gains that can obscure the company's core earnings power — shows an operating loss of more than half a billion dollars in the third quarter. The bottom line: Anthropic still has a long way to go before it is going to be standing on its own feet, financially speaking. 


 
 
   
   
A MESSAGE FROM CAPITAL ONE

 Capital One and the Capital One Foundation's $25M philanthropic initiative aims to scale solutions that expand access to homeownership.


 Looking ahead: Five of 10 finalists will receive $4.6M each in spring 2027 to scale affordable homeownership solutions over the next five years.


 Learn more.
